design_detail: Cross-sectional structural MRI study at 3 T in 22 people with a history of methamphetamine dependence and 21 people without a substance-use history. Cortical pattern matching produced maps of gray-matter density (proportion of gray matter within a 15 mm sphere at each cortical point); hippocampi were traced and modelled for volume and radial size; lobar gray and white matter and ventricles were measured. A four-item memory test was given and correlated with hippocampal measures within the sample.
can_establish: That in this sample, gray-matter density around the right cingulate and limbic cortex was lower, hippocampal volumes smaller and white-matter volume larger than in these controls, and that hippocampal size covaried with word recall.
cannot_establish: That methamphetamine caused any of these differences (no pre-use scan; groups differ in education, smoking and depressive symptoms), that the differences are progressive or reversible (one scan), or that the participants' memory was impaired relative to controls or norms (no group comparison of the memory scores is reported).

sample.recruitment: Not stated in this paper; selection criteria are referred to the companion PET paper (London et al., 2004). Participants screened at UCLA; a partially overlapping subsample (17 users, 18 controls) had PET in that study (Materials and Methods › Participants; Figure 1 legend).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Both groups healthy on examination, history and laboratory tests. Excluded: psychoactive medication; cardiovascular, pulmonary or systemic disease; HIV seropositivity. By SCID-I, any current Axis I diagnosis other than methamphetamine or nicotine dependence excluded users; controls could have no lifetime substance-use diagnosis and no current Axis I disorder. Axis II disorders were not exclusionary (Materials and Methods › Participants).
sample.demographics: Table 1 (means with SEM): age 31.9 (1.47) in controls vs 35.3 (1.66) in users; 10 of 21 controls and 15 of 22 users were men; education 15.2 (0.50) vs 12.8 (0.42) years, p<0.001; mother's education 14.2 (0.48, n=20) vs 13.0 (0.68); race and handedness similar. Table 3: Beck Depression Inventory 1.25 (1.25, n=20) vs 9.77 (1.89), p<0.0005; Spielberger state anxiety 31.4 (3.77) vs 38.67 (2.64) in 15 per group, reported as not significant (p=0.0506); trait anxiety 31.9 (2.41) vs 38.7 (2.63), reported p<0.001.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single session), but Table 2 shows incomplete drug-use data (duration n=21, weekly amount n=19, age of first use n=12 of 22) and Table 3 incomplete questionnaire data (anxiety in 15 per group).
sample.selection_effects: A dependent, mostly tobacco-smoking group with markedly more depressive symptoms and about 2.4 fewer years of education (editors' calculation from the printed SEMs: standardized difference about 1.1 for education and about 1.1 for depression scores) compared with screened healthy volunteers. Recruitment source is not reported in this paper, so the selection route cannot be judged.

exposure.measurement: Self-report only: an intake questionnaire, a drug-use survey and the Addiction Severity Index; DSM-IV dependence by SCID-I. No toxicological verification is described in this paper (Materials and Methods › Drug use).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported, Table 2: 10.5 years of use (SEM 1.09, n=21), about 3.44 g per week (SEM 0.79, n=19), used on 18.9 of the previous 30 days (SEM 1.75, n=21), first use at 26.1 years (SEM 1.77, n=12); route primarily smoking (stated in the text, not tabulated). Reported as study-sample characteristics.
exposure.polysubstance: Tobacco: 15 of 22 users vs 2 of 21 controls smoked more than 5 cigarettes a day (p<0.001 by the editors' Fisher test). Cannabis: 2.38 vs 0.14 days in the previous 30 (p<0.05). Alcohol days similar (3.24 vs 2.38). Six users with heavy cannabis use or cannabis dependence were removed in sensitivity analyses, which did not change significance. Smoking was acknowledged as a limitation but not adjusted for (Materials and Methods › Drug use; Discussion, limitations paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Mean 6.64 days (SD 5.2), printed only in the mood table; how abstinence was established or verified is not described in this paper (Table 3).

comparison.controls: 21 screened volunteers with no history of substance abuse (Materials and Methods › Participants).
comparison.matching: Described as age-matched; not matched on sex (10 of 21 vs 15 of 22 men), education, smoking or mood. Hippocampal analyses adjusted for age and sex and, separately, for brain size; the cortical maps are described as a regression on group membership, with no covariates stated.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use imaging or cognitive baseline; current education and mother's education are the only proxies for premorbid circumstances, and education differed.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: No lifetime substance-use diagnosis; 2 smoked tobacco and cannabis use was minimal.

outcomes.instruments: 3 T GE scanner, 3D T1-weighted SPGR (1.22 mm slices); automated tissue segmentation; cortical surface extraction and cortical pattern matching using 30 sulci per hemisphere traced by an analyst blind to diagnosis, sex and age; gray-matter density as the proportion of gray matter within a 15 mm sphere; hippocampal surface models with radial distance from a central axis; lobar gray and white matter and ventricular volumes. Memory: a repeated memory test with 25 words and 25 line drawings, tested after a 10-minute distraction, giving word recall, picture recall, word recognition and picture recognition. Mood: Beck Depression Inventory and State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (Materials and Methods).
outcomes.validity_norms: Gray-matter density is a local proportion measure, not cortical thickness or volume, although the text also calls the same 11.3% figure a difference in gray-matter volume. Memory scores are raw counts correct; no norms are applied and no group comparison of memory is reported.
outcomes.operationalization: Deficit was defined as a lower group mean in a structural measure; impaired memory performance in the abstract rests on a within-sample correlation between hippocampal measures and word recall.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Cortical and hippocampal maps: permutation testing with 1,000,000 permutations giving one corrected p per map; lateral-surface maps were not significant after correction. Volumetric tests (hippocampus total and by side, with and without brain-size adjustment; ventricles; total and hemispheric white matter; four lobar white-matter regions; total gray matter) are reported uncorrected. The four memory correlations were Bonferroni-corrected for the left-hippocampus radial analysis (p=0.01 uncorrected, p<0.05 corrected).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The analyst who traced sulci was blind to group, sex and age; blinding for hippocampal tracing is referred to earlier methods and not restated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Reported as percentage differences with p-values; no means, SDs or standardized effect sizes are printed for the brain measures (volumes appear only in Figure 3, an image), so standardized differences cannot be computed by the editors. Cortical gray matter: cingulate, subgenual and paralimbic region 11.3% below controls (p<0.05 in the Results; the Figure 1 and Figure 3 legends give p<0.034, corrected); adjacent medial frontal cortex 3.6% lower (p<0.1); left cingulate 0.7% lower (p=0.4 in the Results, p>0.1 in the Lateralization section); lateral surfaces not significant after correction. Hippocampus: 7.8% smaller overall (p<0.01), left 8.2% (p=0.01), right 7.5% (p<0.05), adjusted for age and sex, and still significant after adjustment for brain size and after excluding the 6 heavy cannabis users. White matter: 7.0% larger overall (p<0.01), left 6.6% (p=0.01), right 7.5% (p<0.01 in the Results, p<0.001 in the Discussion), with temporal (left p<0.005, right p<0.05) and occipital (left p<0.05, right p<0.01) excess; mean net white-matter gain 24.3 cc against a mean gray-matter reduction of 6.3 cc. Right frontal horn of the lateral ventricle 25.2% larger (p<0.05). No group difference in total cerebral volume or total gray matter (p>0.1). Memory: total and right hippocampal volume correlated positively with word recall (both p<0.05; coefficients not printed); left hippocampal radial atrophy related to group (p<0.05) and to word recall (p=0.01, p<0.05 corrected); picture recall and both recognition measures were not related to hippocampal measures.
analysis.covariates: Age and sex in the hippocampal volume regressions; brain size in a secondary analysis; cannabis handled by exclusion in a sensitivity analysis. No adjustment for education, tobacco smoking or depressive symptoms, all of which differed between groups; covariates for the cortical maps are not stated.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Two regions were predicted in advance from the companion PET study (cingulate) and from the memory literature (hippocampus), but no registration exists.
analysis.selective_reporting: Memory scores are used only in correlations; the groups' memory performance is never compared. Correlation coefficients are not given for the hippocampal-volume analyses. Percentages are reported without SDs or confidence intervals.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 22 and 21 participants, only differences of roughly one standard deviation or more are reliably detectable; the authors note that correlations with other cognitive measures might appear in a larger cohort.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A cross-sectional pattern of lower right cingulate and limbic gray-matter density, smaller hippocampi, larger white-matter volume and a larger right frontal horn in 22 people who had used methamphetamine than in 21 controls who were better educated, mostly non-smoking and much less depressed, with hippocampal size correlating with word recall within the sample.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that the maps suggest chronic methamphetamine abuse causes a selective pattern of cerebral deterioration that contributes to impaired memory performance, and that methamphetamine may selectively damage the medial temporal lobe and cingulate-limbic cortex; it also offers therapeutic targets for drug-induced brain injury. The title is descriptive, but the discussion compares the changes with early dementia and schizophrenia in effect size, calls the hippocampi severely atrophied, and describes neurodegeneration. None of this follows from one cross-sectional scan: there is no baseline, no adjustment for education, smoking or depression, and no demonstration that these participants' memory was worse than controls'. The discussion acknowledges that it is unknown whether the deficits are progressive or reversible, and that the smoking imbalance is a limitation, but argues from one published smoking study that the pattern differs.

timeline.event: Companion PET study in a partially overlapping sample reported cingulate and limbic metabolic differences correlated with self-reported mood (London et al., 2004, as cited here).
An independent sample recruited within an HIV study was reported in abstract form to show enlarged lobar volumes (Jernigan et al., 2003, as cited here).
Gray-matter volume compared in people using methamphetamine with and without cigarette smoking, and with abstinence (Morales et al., 2012; appraised in this batch).

replication.where_it_stands: Smaller limbic and hippocampal gray matter in people who use methamphetamine has been reported repeatedly, but the smoking confound was not separated here; the white-matter excess has had little replication, and whether the differences precede use or change with abstinence is unresolved.

funding.funder: US National Institute on Drug Abuse contract Y01 DA50038 (E.D.L., W.L.) and grant R01 DA15179 (E.D.L.); National Center for Research Resources M01 RR00865; algorithm development by NIBIB and NCRR grants R21 EB01651 and R21 RR019771 (P.M.T.); a Human Brain Project grant to the International Consortium for Brain Mapping funded by NIMH and NIDA (P20 MH/DA52176, P41 RR13642) (Footnotes).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: UCLA Laboratory of Neuroimaging and departments of psychiatry and pharmacology. The imaging method (cortical pattern matching) is the senior imaging authors' own; the comparison PET map in Figure 1 comes from the same group's companion study. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Longitudinal MRI in people before and after the onset of regular methamphetamine use, with a non-using comparison group scanned at the same intervals, tobacco-smoking and education matched or adjusted, and the memory battery administered to both groups against norms; or at minimum a cross-sectional study with a smoking control group, as later attempted by Morales et al. (2012).

domains.note: Education (about 2.4 years), tobacco smoking (15 of 22 vs 2 of 21) and depressive symptoms all differ and none is adjusted for; cortical map covariates are not stated; no pre-use measurement.
Self-report only, with no toxicology described in this paper; key exposure variables are missing for some participants (weekly amount n=19, age of first use n=12 of 22).
Recruitment source is not reported here; dependent users against screened healthy volunteers; sample partly overlaps the group's earlier PET study.
Abstinence averaged 6.64 days with a wide spread (SD 5.2) and no stated verification; any acute withdrawal effect on tissue water or volume is not addressed.
Mood and drug-use data are incomplete for several participants; anxiety measures from only 15 per group.
Blinded sulcal tracing and automated segmentation, but gray-matter density is a derived proportional measure reported interchangeably with volume.

Memory scores reported only as correlations with brain measures, never as a group comparison; correlation coefficients omitted; volumetric tests reported uncorrected while the maps are corrected; figure legends and text give different p-values for the same results.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The imaging methods are careful and the maps are permutation-corrected, but the design cannot separate drug effects from education, tobacco smoking and depression, and the central clinical claim (impaired memory) rests on a within-group correlation with no group comparison of the memory test.

key_findings.finding: Gray-matter density in a cingulate, subgenual and paralimbic region was 11.3% lower in 22 people who had used methamphetamine than in 21 controls, with the effect on the right medial surface; the overall cortical map was significant after permutation correction.
key_findings.locator: Results › Mapping cortical gray-matter deficits; Figures 1 and 3e
key_findings.note: Results text gives p<0.05; the Figure 1 and Figure 3 legends give p<0.034 corrected.

key_findings.finding: Left cingulate gray-matter density was 0.7% lower (not significant), and adjacent medial frontal cortex 3.6% lower (p<0.1); lateral-surface differences did not survive correction.
key_findings.locator: Results › Mapping cortical gray-matter deficits; Lateralization section; Figure 2

key_findings.finding: Hippocampal volume was 7.8% smaller overall (p<0.01), 8.2% on the left (p=0.01) and 7.5% on the right (p<0.05), adjusted for age and sex; the difference persisted after adjusting for brain size and after excluding 6 participants with heavy cannabis use.

Total white-matter volume was 7.0% larger in the methamphetamine group (p<0.01; left 6.6%, right 7.5%), with temporal and occipital excess; mean net white-matter gain 24.3 cc against a mean gray-matter reduction of 6.3 cc.
key_findings.locator: Results › Whole-brain gray- and white-matter measures; Discussion, white-matter paragraph

key_findings.finding: The right frontal horn of the lateral ventricle was 25.2% larger (p<0.05); total cerebral volume and total gray matter did not differ (p>0.1).
key_findings.locator: Results › Whole-brain gray- and white-matter measures

key_findings.finding: Hippocampal volume (total and right) correlated with word recall (both p<0.05), and left hippocampal radial atrophy correlated with word recall (p=0.01, p<0.05 after Bonferroni correction for four memory tests); picture recall and word and picture recognition showed no relation.
key_findings.note: Correlation coefficients are not printed; only p-values.

key_findings.finding: The memory test scores were never compared between the groups; the paper reports no test of whether the methamphetamine group recalled fewer words than controls.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Neuropsychological testing; Results › Hippocampal deficits

key_findings.finding: Group characteristics: users had 12.8 vs 15.2 years of education (p<0.001), 15 of 22 vs 2 of 21 smoked more than 5 cigarettes a day, Beck Depression Inventory 9.77 vs 1.25 (p<0.0005), and had been abstinent a mean of 6.64 days (SD 5.2) by self-report.

Self-reported use: about 10.5 years, about 3.44 g per week, on 18.9 of the previous 30 days, primarily by smoking; exposure data were missing for some participants (weekly amount reported for 19 of 22, age of first use for 12 of 22).
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Materials and Methods › Drug use

key_findings.finding: Editors' calculation from the printed means and SEMs: standardized group differences of about 1.1 for education and about 1.1 for depression scores, and about 0.5 for age (not significant), indicating that the groups differ on these variables about as strongly as the brain measures differ.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: SEM converted to SD, Hedges' g with pooled SD.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results refer to Figure 2b, 2c and 2d for ventricular, gray-matter and white-matter volumes, but those panels are in Figure 3; Figure 2 shows lateral-surface maps.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results › Whole-brain gray- and white-matter measures)
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers checking the volumetric data are sent to the wrong figure.

reporting_issues.issue: The right-hemisphere white-matter excess is given as 7.5% with p<0.01 in the Results and p<0.001 in the Discussion.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two p-values is wrong; the finding's strength is uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: The cingulate deficit is reported as p<0.05 in the Results but p<0.034 corrected in the Figure 1 and Figure 3 legends; the left cingulate is p=0.4 in the Results and p>0.1 in the Lateralization section.
reporting_issues.consequence: Inconsistent reporting of the same tests.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1 the significance marker also appears on the mother's education row, implying p<0.001; from the printed means and SEMs (14.2 vs 13.0) the difference is about t=1.4, p≈0.16 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The asterisk appears to be misplaced; readers could conclude the groups differed strongly in parental education.

reporting_issues.issue: Trait anxiety is marked p<0.001 (31.9 vs 38.7, SEM 2.41 and 2.63, 15 per group); from those figures the editors calculate t≈1.9, p≈0.07. State anxiety is given as p=0.0506 where the same calculation gives p≈0.13.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the printed statistics or the sample sizes are wrong; the mood differences between groups cannot be verified as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The same 11.3% figure is described as gray-matter density in the Methods and Lateralization section and as gray-matter volume in the abstract and Results.
reporting_issues.consequence: Density here is a proportion within a 15 mm sphere; calling it volume overstates what was measured.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 reports drug-use variables for different subsets (duration n=21, weekly amount n=19, age of first use n=12) without explaining the missing data; Table 3 reports anxiety for 15 of each group.
reporting_issues.consequence: Exposure characterization rests on partial data, and the mood comparison on two-thirds of the sample.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract describes the groups as age-matched, but the sex ratio differs (15 of 22 men vs 10 of 21) and age differs by 3.4 years in the same direction as the structural findings.
reporting_issues.consequence: Sex and age are adjusted in the hippocampal analyses but their handling in the cortical maps is not stated.

reporting_issues.issue: No toxicological verification of abstinence or of control status is described in this paper; abstinence appears only as a row in the mood table.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Materials and Methods › Drug use; Table 3)
reporting_issues.consequence: Recent use at the time of scanning cannot be excluded from the information given here.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC6729247 (all sections, Tables 1–3 as text, all four figure legends; Figures 1–4 are images of maps and bar charts, so the volumes plotted in Figure 3 could not be extracted; no supplementary material)
